about: The evidence behind one statement, row by row. Authored by researcher@php.newsroom on 22 October 2026 at the editor's request. Each row says who said what, when, in their words, and where the capture is: 'sources' are evidence-vault slugs the gate checks; 'watch' is a dated snapshot folder in the source-watch vault (7r83qic5), held there until the evidence curator promotes it. This file maps evidence; it makes no assessment of risk.
statement: No named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell.
status_note: A time-bounded absence, not a confirmed fact. It is true only as of the last check, and one statement from one organisation would end it. A vendor's report of unnamed victims (Dream Research, 26 October; row below) names no organisation or victim, and no victim, vendor, CISA or PHP-team statement confirms it, so it does not end the statement; it is carried as a report.

kinds.name: Exploitation reported, no victim named

kinds.name: No successful exploitation known

kinds.cannot: that nothing happened outside its view

kinds.name: Official exploited signals
kinds.cannot: anything they have not yet recorded

rows.says: An exploit attempt against a MadPot honeypot four days before disclosure; "it's unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems."
First sensor hit, about 55 minutes after Chainguard's images.
"We observed attack traffic targeting our customers" and attackers "mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections".
First in-the-wild attempts hit its sensors; "Whilst nobody has been successful to date, we don't expect that will last long."
Automated exploitation attempts seen in Latvia; no successful attacks reported.
"thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now."
"At least one Chinese IP address unsuccessfully attempted to exploit PHP2Shell to deploy a webshell."
Observed scanning activity and attack attempts using the PHP2Shell flaws.

rows.who: A Tencent News analyst, with ThreatBook sensors (China)
rows.says: Captured scanning requests with the User-Agent php2shell-scan/1.0; no evidence of successful code execution.
"We are now seeing php2shell exploited in the wild at scale." No victim named.
"Received reports of multiple active exploitation incidents from hosting partners." No victim named.
"PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild." Against its sensors; no victim named.
"The NCSC is aware of reports of active exploitation." Whose reports is not said.
"CISA has not observed exploitation of these vulnerabilities as of the time of publication."
"As of October 21 at 4:30pm ET, Huntress has not observed in-the-wild exploitation on partner systems."
The security team "did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release/public disclosure."

rows.who: The PHP Foundation's executive director (to The Verge and WIRED)
rows.says: "To our knowledge, there has been no successful attempt at remote code execution."

rows.who: Germany's BSI, the Dutch NCSC, Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary (via The Next Web, Politico)
rows.says: Germany has seen attacks but no successful use; the Netherlands has no indication of active misuse; Japan says no attacks exploiting the flaws have been confirmed.
Knows of no attacks in Switzerland attributable to the flaws (via SRF, read in German).
Has recorded no attacks on Belgian websites (via RTVE, read in Spanish; and Clickx, in French).
No concrete reports of successful attacks so far (via Salzburg24, read in German).
Its observations "describe attack attempts; they do not, by themselves, establish successful compromises."

Malicious programs were found on 20 October on servers of its FX trading VPS service; 26,739 servers possibly affected; account logins may have been taken; fraudulent operations reported. The cause is not stated.
rows.reading: A confirmed break-in, cause not stated

rows.says: Facing "a cyber attack on its IT infrastructure… part of worldwide attempts to hit PHP sites"; "the active attack was stopped"; some systems taken offline.
rows.reading: An attack reported and stopped; success not stated

rows.says: First blamed a "cyberattack targeting the PHP vulnerability", then corrected: the attackers used a flaw in its own service.
rows.reading: Attribution to php2shell retracted

rows.says: Halted services to respond to "a vulnerability in external software"; no data leaked; would not say whether it was PHP.
rows.reading: Precaution; cause not stated

rows.says: Its site "was not hacked", only taken down "for a repair".
rows.reading: Precaution, stated not compromised

rows.says: Confirmed attack attempts on websites it operates; bank data not affected (via ORF).
rows.reading: Attempts, stated not compromised

rows.says: No reason to believe its recent cyberattack is linked to the PHP flaws (via Accountant.nl).
rows.reading: A separate incident, link denied

rows.says: Alleges hackers stole source code, exposed cookie data and leaked legal documents. Unnamed; not attributed to php2shell; not verified.
Version 2026.10.21, 1,754 entries; neither CVE listed. The source watch re-read it at 08:03 UTC on 23 October, unchanged since its capture at 18:16 UTC on 22 October.

rows.who: CISA's assessment on the CVE records (SSVC)
rows.says: Exploitation: none. Automatable: no. Technical impact: total.
0.053 and 0.058: the modelled probability of exploitation activity in the next 30 days.
In its critical alert, ASD's ACSC said it was "not aware of active exploitation related to these vulnerabilities".

"Shortly after PHP's update, our telemetry shows only probing attacks, with no hard evidence of breaches yet." Recorded Future reports the same company receiving reports of exploitation incidents from hosting partners that morning; the two accounts are not reconciled.

No Luxembourg financial institution, public service or operator had announced it had actually been infiltrated through php2shell; the state announced no confirmed compromise, and the authorities asked operators to search back for traces of compromise and to keep the evidence.
rows.reading: An absence of announcements, not a finding

rows.says: An exploitation attempt tried to deploy Potassium, a likely Mirai botnet variant; security controls blocked it and the malware was not delivered.

In a correction issued at 21:21 UTC on 22 October, Sophos said its customer data showed scanning and a small number of failed exploit attempts, and no evidence of a successful compromise; an earlier success claim was withdrawn.
rows.reading: A vendor's success claim, made and withdrawn

rows.who: US banks and credit unions (via American Banker)
rows.says: "Attackers have fired millions of attempts at the PHP2Shell flaws, but no U.S. bank or credit union has publicly reported a compromise."
rows.reading: An absence of public reports, not a finding

rows.who: Crypto exchanges and payment providers (via BTC-ECHO)
rows.says: No evidence so far that large crypto trading platforms or payment providers were compromised through php2shell.
rows.reading: An absence of evidence, reported by a trade outlet

rows.says: As of 12:03 Vienna time (10:03 UTC) on 23 October 2026 no successful attacks via PHP2Shell were known in Austria.
rows.reading: A point-in-time absence, reported by a newspaper

rows.says: RainForest's honeypot network matched 3 of 11 public IP addresses from VulnCheck and Amazon threat information and recorded 21 PHP2Shell-related HTTP POST requests, from 14 different source IPs.
rows.reading: A small honeypot sample: attempts, not intrusions

rows.who: Turkey's Presidency Cybersecurity Directorate (via Haber and three other Turkish outlets)
rows.says: Said the e-Devlet Kapisi government portal, with more than 69 million users, had no security problem from PHP2Shell and that services continued uninterrupted.
rows.reading: An organisation's statement about its own portal, as four news sites relay it; the Directorate's own post is not among the captures (searched the text of every capture for its name and 'e-Devlet')

rows.who: La Razón (Spain), on the investigations it cites
rows.says: As of 23 October 2026 attempts against PHP2Shell were real and in the millions, but no successful code execution had been established in the investigations cited.
rows.reading: A point-in-time absence, reported by a newspaper

rows.who: Amazon Threat Intelligence (via ZDNET Japan, translating ZDNET)
rows.says: Threat actors in PHP2Shell attack chains are trying to deploy Mirai-family botnets.
rows.reading: Attempts, no named actor; reported on 26 October. Amazon's own post in the vault does not contain the word 'Mirai'. The English ZDNET page (27 October capture) says the same without naming a source or an actor

rows.who: ScaleCommerce (Germany, a hosting provider, in its own press release)
rows.says: Its log review found only isolated attack attempts on customer shops and no indications of a broad compromise.
rows.reading: One provider's own account of its own customers

rows.who: Square Enix (Japan), as TechGaming.it reports it, citing Kotaku
rows.says: Square Enix 'confirmed episodes of unauthorised access to its systems' in the same week as PHP2Shell.
rows.reading: Unverified, second-hand: the outlet does not say the access came through the PHP flaws, and Kotaku's text and Square Enix's own words are not captured. Bitpage, the other page that names Square Enix, says it closed new Final Fantasy XIV logins and took patch servers offline, with the cause 'not an attack' but the PHP flaws

rows.who: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and CISA's alert of 26 October
rows.says: Both CVEs added to the catalog on 26 October 2026 (version 2026.10.26, released at 22:24 UTC, 1,758 entries): CISA "has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog", and an addition must have "evidence of exploitation". Due date for US federal civilian agencies: 29 October. Known ransomware use: "Unknown". The alert and the two entries name no victim, no compromised organisation and no threat actor. The catalog page, as served at 19:13 UTC on 27 October, shows the same two entries (forensic triage required "Yes"; 1,760 entries by then), still naming no victim.
rows.reading: Exploited in the wild, on CISA's evidence; no compromised organisation named

rows.who: Adel Karimi (Perplexity), with honeypots; Marcus Hutchins (Expel) on it (via ENTER.CO, citing BleepingComputer)
rows.says: Honeypots recorded a successful remote code execution against Apache with mod_php and PHP 8.4.26: the attacker obtained server memory and then ran a command. Hutchins called it the best-quality confirmation of exploitation he had seen.
rows.reading: A decoy server on a vulnerable build (8.4.26 is below the fixed 8.4.27), not an organisation; one page, and the BleepingComputer article is not among the captures. No victim named. Europe Infos (26 October, unattributed) gives the same decoy result in numbers: 35 malicious PHP shells launched by Apache processes on three PHP 8.4.26 test servers, first on 24 October. SC Media (26 October) adds, through Suzu Labs' Calderone, that Karimi recorded 35 working shells on unpatched PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php, with packet-to-process evidence tying each captured request to a shell spawned by an Apache worker, in a deliberately favourable single-worker setup: it proves exploitation is real, not that it works reliably everywhere. The Hacker News (27 October) dates the decoy result to 24 October and quotes Karimi's own limit: "The evidence demonstrates this chain on the intentionally favorable single-worker mod_php profile; it is not a measurement of exploit reliability on other worker counts, PHP builds, or applications." THN says CISA's KEV addition "comes after" it: THN's sequence, not a reason CISA gave.

rows.who: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (via SC Media)
rows.says: In an Oct. 25 blog Unit 42 retracted its Oct. 23 statement that an attack against a European government agency was related to a vulnerable PHP2Shell application, saying it was unable to confirm that initial access was associated with either of the two bugs.
rows.reading: A vendor's attribution, made and withdrawn (as Sophos's was); no agency named; the original statement and Unit 42's blog are not captured, only SC Media's account of them

rows.says: In an Oct. 26 blog Sophos said that, as of its reporting, PHP2Shell had yet to become the mass exploitation event many in the industry braced for.
rows.reading: A vendor's own view of what it sees, second-hand; Sophos's blog is not captured

rows.who: watchTowr's head of threat intelligence, Jake Knott (via SC Media)
rows.says: Whether reliable, indiscriminate exploitation is happening in the wild: 'for now, the answer is a firm No'. SC Media adds that as of the afternoon of 26 October there were no known public reports of successful exploitation and no widespread exploitation.
rows.reading: A vendor's reading and the outlet's, at one moment; CISA's KEV listing of 26 October is the position that the flaws are exploited

rows.who: Delft Threat Intelligence Lab, as Suzu Labs' Denis Calderone gives it to SC Media
rows.says: Honeypots and a network telescope recorded more than 50,000 PHP2Shell exploitation requests from more than 600 addresses in 70 countries as of the morning of 26 October; the busiest hour so far brought more than 5,100 requests; 171 of the addresses had moved past probing to sending code or droppers.
rows.reading: Attempt volume, not successful compromise; second-hand through Suzu Labs

rows.who: Cyfirma (via Money Today, 24 October; CNET France, 27 October, relaying The Hacker News)
rows.says: A reconnaissance campaign tied to the Lazarus ecosystem at medium confidence, named 'June 2026 Minjun': on 22 October the operators targeted government bodies and banks in the US, Japan, South Korea, the UAE, the EU, Thailand, Indonesia and Saudi Arabia, then manufacturing, logistics, shipping, airports and other sectors; Cyfirma saw 17 suspect source addresses doing web shell tooling and upload-progress session poisoning attempts within eight hours. CNET France adds that 21 already-compromised servers were used to examine 216 potentially vulnerable targets.
rows.reading: Preparation and probing, attributed with medium confidence; Money Today says no actual compromise was found. The 21 and 216 figures are on the CNET France page only. No victim named

rows.who: CNET France, 27 October (the developer of StealMyBitcoin.com; Sixactualités 26 October gives 19.28 hours)
rows.says: A developer left a PHP server deliberately unpatched at StealMyBitcoin.com with more than 2,000 dollars in bitcoin as the prize; about 20 hours after the challenge launched a participant exploited the flaws and took it.
rows.reading: A deliberate challenge target, not an organisation and not a victim; reported on 26 and 27 October by two outlets and not by the developer in the vault. No victim named

rows.who: Park Se-jun, chief executive of Theori, in an interview with ZDNet Korea
rows.says: Attempts are real, but a distinction has to be kept between attempts and successful intrusions: Sophos and Palo Alto Networks first announced successful attacks and later corrected or withdrew them, and Palo Alto's government-agency case was not confirmed to have begun with the PHP flaw. The honeypot success is a lab, not a company. As of 27 October no publicly verified breach of a real company or institution had been confirmed; unknown damage cannot be excluded.
rows.reading: One security executive's reading of the public record, in an interview; not a count of what attackers have done

rows.who: Zscaler ThreatLabz (via Fortune India, 27 October; Zscaler's own post is not in the vault)
rows.says: Its global decoy network observed 1,156 exploitation attempts from 156 unique attacker IP addresses targeting 70 organisations in the first 48 hours after the 21 October disclosure, including scanning and possible exploitation with several tools and code-execution payloads.
rows.reading: Attempt volume against a decoy network, not a compromise; 'organisations' is the outlet's word. Second-hand, on this page only. No victim named

rows.who: CERT.LV (Latvia), as Jauns.lv / LETA report it on 27 October; the deputy head, Varis Teivans, said the same on 22 October (Delfi)
rows.says: No successful cyberattack exploiting the critical PHP flaws had been recorded in Latvia so far, and no incidents tied to their exploitation had been found; attacker activity could grow and tools improve. About 6,000 potentially vulnerable resources were found, a few hundred of them public-sector.
rows.reading: What the national CERT has seen in Latvia, not a statement about elsewhere. No victim named

rows.who: Craft CMS (Pixel & Tonic), on its blog
rows.says: "While there is evidence that the vulnerabilities were being exploited even before the PHP updates were released, sites protected by Cloudflare’s firewalls were protected." Craft does not say what the evidence is or whose.
rows.reading: Exploitation before the fixes, on Craft's word; no evidence shown, no victim named, and no Craft Cloud site said to be compromised

rows.who: Craft CMS, on the sites it hosts (Craft Cloud)
rows.says: Cloudflare's emergency firewall rules "have effectively protected Craft Cloud-hosted sites, with no known successful attacks"; save "a small handful of sites with preexisting build issues", every Cloud environment was moved to patched PHP images the same day.
rows.reading: What a host has seen on its own platform, not elsewhere. No victim named

rows.says: "NETGEAR has not seen any evidence of exploits targeting these devices": six Nighthawk models (RAX28, RAX29, RAX30, RAXE290, RAXE300, CAX30) include PHP for local management, "not accessible from the Internet by default"; their impact is under review.
rows.reading: A vendor on its own devices. No victim named

rows.who: Broadcom (its PHP2Shell response page, last updated 23 October)
rows.says: "Isolated exposures were promptly mitigated, our security solutions were tuned to detect and prevent exploitation attempts, and no compromise of any infrastructure has been discovered." Ten products have potential exposure (three in the Enterprise Security Group, four in Identity Management Security, three in Tanzu), and their teams are releasing fixes.
rows.reading: A vendor on its own infrastructure: exposures mitigated, no compromise found

rows.who: Arista Networks (Security Advisory 0200, 23 October, revised 26 October)
rows.says: "Arista is not aware of any malicious exploitation of these vulnerabilities in customer networks." No Arista software product is presently impacted; its CloudVision CUE service and Arista Edge Threat Management were, and have been upgraded.
rows.reading: What a vendor knows of its customers' networks. No victim named

rows.says: Splunk fixed its Smartlook service by upgrading PHP, and "Splunk has not found evidence of exploitation"; products not listed in the advisory are not affected.
rows.reading: A vendor on its own service. No victim named

rows.who: Salesforce (Trust message 20000267, 21 October, updated 16:08 UTC on 27 October)
rows.says: "At this time, we have no evidence of exploitation affecting Salesforce or customer data" and "We have seen no evidence of compromise of Salesforce customers or data"; no Salesforce product is affected except Informatica, where expedited patching is in progress.
rows.reading: A vendor on its own systems and its customers' data. No victim named

rows.who: Dream Research (dreamgroup.com, a security vendor that sells the tooling it says it used), in its post of 26 October; repeated on 28 October by The Hacker News, The Next Web and CyPro (which credits SecurityWeek)
rows.says: Dream says a campaign chaining CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with a Linux kernel flaw (CVE-2026-46300) rooted 25 servers in the United States, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea: 24 firewalls of a large vendor it does not name, plus one internal firewall-management server, with three servers in one US government-affiliated environment. It says it found the artifacts on 25 October, notified the vendor, and cannot tell whether later steps (a password spray, backdoor accounts, signing-key extraction) worked. It names no actor and gives Chinese-nexus indicators only. The Next Web: "TNW has not independently verified Dream's findings." CyPro: other sources "do not independently verify Dream's specific victim details"; it also says SecurityWeek reported two servers at the organisation where Dream says three, a discrepancy it calls unresolved.
rows.reading: Reported by Dream, not independently confirmed. One source: the three outlets repeat Dream's post (CyPro is a relay of SecurityWeek). Dream publishes no artifact and names no victim and no vendor; no vendor, CISA or PHP-team statement about these victims is in the vault. The two PHP2Shell CVE numbers match CISA's KEV listing, which says the flaws are exploited and names no victim; the kernel flaw's number is not in CISA's material. A report of compromise, not a confirmed compromise: no named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell

layers.note: Hadrian, Patchstack, Amazon; no victim named by any

layers.note: ČVUT: attack stopped, success not stated

layers.label: Named organisations saying php2shell was the way in
layers.note: GMO reports a break-in without a cause; Valtec retracted its attribution

layers.note: Dream Research (26 October): 25 servers rooted, three in a US government-affiliated environment; single source, evidence withheld; repeated by The Hacker News, The Next Web and CyPro; no victim, vendor or agency has confirmed it

would_change_it: A named organisation saying it was compromised through php2shell, in its own notice, filing or statement.
GMO, ČVUT or DMM stating a cause.
CISA naming a victim, in its catalog, its updated PHP alert or elsewhere. Its KEV listing of 26 October (both CVEs) holds evidence of exploitation and names none, so it did not change this statement.
A regulator's breach notice (for example under GDPR or Australia's Notifiable Data Breaches scheme) naming the flaw.
A security vendor naming a victim, with the victim's consent.

A named victim, the firewall's vendor, CISA or the US government-affiliated organisation confirming Dream Research's account of 26 October. Dream names no victim and no vendor, and The Next Web says it has not independently verified the findings: the report did not change this statement.
